claims.text: TGA under controlled high-temperature oxidative conditions can quantitatively measure oxidation behaviour through sample weight changes.
TGA can capture phase-stability transitions by monitoring thermal events.
The starting material is in an unoxidized, as-synthesized crystalline state.
High-temperature oxidative exposure forms oxide phases.
Oxide-phase formation produces observable weight gain.
Oxide-phase formation produces thermal responses indicative of phase transitions.
Elevated temperatures induce oxidation reactions that incorporate oxygen into the material.
Oxygen incorporation during oxidation increases sample weight.
Exothermic or endothermic events indicate phase transitions.
The relevant phase transitions can involve changes in lattice structure.
A TGA curve under the proposed conditions will show a distinct weight gain corresponding to oxygen uptake.
If DSC is used, its signal will reveal thermal events corresponding to phase transitions.
The combined weight-gain and thermal-event signals can confirm a link between oxidation kinetics and phase stability.
At lower temperatures or under inert atmospheres, the material should exhibit minimal weight change.
At lower temperatures or under inert atmospheres, the material should exhibit no significant thermal events.
The method is applicable only when the material does not rapidly disintegrate or sublime during high-temperature TGA.
Oxidation must occur at a measurable rate rather than too rapidly for TGA to capture.
Oxidation kinetics and phase-transition temperatures vary with material composition.
Quantitative correlation of oxidation behaviour with phase stability requires prior calibration.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes monitoring of thermal events and phase-stability transitions to TGA, whereas the intervention and predicted outcome assign heat-flow and transition detection to optional DSC. TGA alone measures mass change and does not directly provide a DSC thermal-event signal.
